analysis.one_liner: Creates a new federal commission to regulate major online platforms for competition, consumer protection, and children's safety.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Michael Bennet with one cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Federal Digital Platform Commission, a new agency with roughly the structure of the FCC or FTC, to regulate large online platforms like social media networks, search engines, and e-commerce marketplaces. It would set rules on competition, algorithmic transparency, privacy, age-appropriate design for children, and access for people with disabilities, and would give the commission a formal voice in reviewing mergers involving the biggest platforms. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary users would gain consumer protections, transparency about how platforms rank and recommend content, and age-appropriate design rules aimed at protecting minors. Small businesses that depend on large platforms to reach customers, and would-be competitors, would benefit from interoperability and merger scrutiny. People with disabilities would gain accessibility standards.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a commission with authority to set rules on access, competition, and consumer protections for digital platforms, including standards for age verification and age-appropriate design for children [S2]

Requires designated 'systemically important' platforms to meet standards on data portability, interoperability, algorithmic transparency and audits, content-moderation transparency, and accessibility for people with hearing, speech, or vision impairments [S3]
Gives the commission a formal role in reviewing mergers involving designated platforms, with recommendations the DOJ and FTC must give substantial weight to [S2][S3]
Lets ordinary people and state attorneys general file complaints and sue to enforce the rules, with a no-direct-damage-required complaint process [S3]
Excludes small digital platform businesses from regulation and directs tailoring of rules based on platform size and dominance [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large digital platforms would bear the cost: compliance with new codes and standards, penalties the commission sets to deter violations capped at 15 percent of global annual revenue, and per-day forfeitures for missed reporting. Taxpayers would fund the commission, with appropriations authorized from $100 million rising to $500 million a year through 2032. Users could face tradeoffs such as age-verification requirements that collect more personal data, and platforms argue regulation of recommendation algorithms could reduce content customization.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes up to $500 million a year in taxpayer funding for a brand-new federal agency covering a fast-moving industry, a substantial recurring cost [S3]

The commission may 'forbear' from regulating platforms based on size or market share, and once it declines to enforce a rule, states are barred from applying that rule themselves, which could narrow protections [S3]

Six of the eighteen seats on the standards-writing Code Council are reserved for representatives of digital platforms, including systemically important ones, giving the regulated industry a formal seat in drafting the rules [S3]

Broad authority over algorithms and content-adjacent design raises good-faith concerns about First Amendment limits, regulatory overreach into speech and innovation, and privacy risks from age-verification standards; the bill responds by requiring First Amendment-consistent regulation and a five-year independent review panel to recommend whether the commission should continue [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a sector with documented harms to minors, small businesses, privacy, and local journalism, and it borrows a proven model — sector-specific expert regulation like the FCC or FTC — rather than inventing an untested one. The costs are real but mostly fall on the regulated platforms, and taxpayer cost, while large, is comparable to other major regulators. The weakest points are its breadth (the definition of 'digital platform' is sweeping, though small businesses and news organizations are exempted), the industry's formal seat in writing standards, and the forbearance and state-preemption provisions that give platforms an escape hatch.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 2023 and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet (D-CO), joined by one cosponsor, Sen. Peter Welch (D-VT), introduced the bill on May 18, 2023 [S1][S3][S4]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5]
No further action was ever taken; the bill's only actions in its entire history are its introduction and committee referral [S5]
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without a vote [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large digital platforms are better off: they avoided a dedicated regulator with merger-review leverage, algorithmic transparency mandates, and penalties that could reach 15 percent of global annual revenue. Ordinary users, small businesses on the platforms, and children gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large digital platforms avoided new regulation

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado; bill sponsor

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only senator to do so

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat there for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape can only be inferred from sponsorship: both sponsors were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and the committee that held the bill was majority-Democrat.

industries.industry: Large digital platforms (major social media, search, and e-commerce companies)
industries.note: The bill would subject the biggest platforms to a dedicated regulator, mandatory algorithmic audits and transparency, interoperability and data-portability standards, merger scrutiny, and penalties capped at 15 percent of global annual revenue. Their interest in avoiding these rules runs against the consumer, small-business, and child-safety protections the bill would impose.

The bill exempts small platform businesses from regulation (unless designated systemically important) and would benefit from interoperability standards that make it easier to compete with dominant platforms.
News organizations are excluded from the bill's definition of regulated platforms, and the bill's stated purposes include countering the platforms' role in the collapse of trusted local journalism.
